sections.title: The Prohibition of Ḥelev
sections.html:
The ḥalavim (forbidden fats) are part of the fats in the meat of a domestic animal, and when an animal is offered to God, it is a mitzva to burn its ḥalavim and to sprinkle its blood on the altar. In continuation of this, the Torah forbade eating ḥelev and blood: since the ḥelev is fit to be burnt for God, and the blood is sprinkled on the altar, it is forbidden for Israel to eat them. As it is stated (Vayikra 3:14-17): "And the sons of Aharon shall dash its blood against the altar round about. And he shall present from it his offering, an offering made by fire to the Lord: the fat that covers the innards, and all the fat that is on the innards, and the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the loins… And the priest shall make them go up in smoke upon the altar; it is the food of the offering made by fire, for a pleasing odour; all the fat is the Lord's. It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings, that you shall eat neither fat nor blood" (the prohibition of blood will be explained in the next chapter).

The prohibition of ḥelev applies to the three species of domestic animal – cattle, sheep and goats – which are fit for a sacrifice, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:23): "Speak to the children of Israel, saying: You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat." But there is no prohibition of ḥelev in the fats of the seven species of kosher wild animal (ḥaya), since sacrifices are not brought from the species of wild animal. Likewise, there is no prohibition of ḥelev in the species of kosher fowl, and even though there are species of fowl that are fit for a sacrifice, their fats have no special status, since a bird brought as an ola (burnt offering) is offered in its entirety on the altar, and in a bird brought as a ḥatat (sin offering) – all of its meat is eaten by the kohanim (Ḥullin 117a). The prohibition is to eat ḥelev, but it is permitted to derive benefit from it and to make use of it for work and for trade (below 37:10).

There is extra severity in the prohibitions of ḥelev and blood: the punishment for other forbidden foods, such as impure animals and sheratzim (creeping creatures), is lashes, whereas the punishment for one who eats ḥelev or blood is karet (spiritual excision), because they are fit to go up on the altar as an offering to God, and one who eats them disgraces sacred things and cuts his soul off from the source of its life. As it is stated (Vayikra 7:25-27): "For whoever eats the fat of the animal of which men present an offering made by fire to the Lord, the soul that eats it shall be cut off from its people… Whatever soul it is that eats any blood, that soul shall be cut off from its people."1

sections.title: What Is Ḥelev
sections.html:
The ḥalavim resemble the fats (shumanim) of the animal in their appearance and texture, except that the ḥalavim are compact and relatively large pieces of fat that are found in three places in the animal, and it is relatively easy to remove them in one piece (SA 64:4), and when a sacrifice is offered we were commanded to burn them on the altar. The shumanim, by contrast, are more absorbed within the meat and it is difficult to remove them in one piece, and when a shelamim (peace offering) is offered, they are eaten together with the meat of the sacrifice. Since the ḥalavim and the shumanim are similar, once they have been cut and separated from the meat of the animal it is difficult to distinguish between them; therefore, eating a piece that is possibly shuman and possibly ḥelev is the common example of eating something of doubtful prohibition, for whose atonement one must bring an 'asham talui' (provisional guilt offering) (Mishna Keritot 4:1).

The meaning of the word ḥelev is choice, excellent and rich. As Pharaoh said to Yosef when he asked him to bring Yaakov his father and his brothers to Egypt: "And I will give you the good of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat the fat (ḥelev) of the land" (Bereishit 45:18). And as is stated regarding Hevel, who brought a sacrifice from the choicest of his flock: "And Hevel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of their fat (ḥelev); and the Lord had respect for Hevel and for his offering" (ibid. 4:4). Likewise, in giving teruma to the kohen, we were commanded to set aside the good part of the produce, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:30): "When you set apart its best (ḥelbo) from it."

It turns out, then, that the ḥelev of the animal is the rich and good part of the animal, since fat is the softest part and the richest in calories, and the ḥalavim are the fine pieces of fat; therefore we were commanded to offer them on the altar. There are three kinds of ḥalavim: 1) The ḥelev on the innards (kerev) – on the digestive stomachs, which are called innards (kera'ayim). 2) The ḥelev on the kidneys. 3) The ḥelev on the kesalim – on the sides of the loins, near the ḥelev on the kidneys. As it is stated (Vayikra 3:3-5): "And he shall present of the sacrifice of the peace offerings an offering made by fire to the Lord: the fat that covers the innards, and all the fat that is on the innards, and the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the loins…"2

sections.title: The Laws of Ḥelev in Practice
sections.html:
Two definitions were stated regarding ḥelev. The first: "spread out, with a membrane, and peelable" (totav, kerum ve-nikhlaf), that is, it is spread like a garment, and it has a membrane such that when it is peeled off, the ḥelev is peeled off with it (Ḥullin 49b). The second: whatever the meat covers, so that it appears absorbed within the meat, is shuman and is permitted (ibid. 93a).

The Sages added and forbade also fats that are attached to and extend from these ḥalavim, even though they are absorbed in the meat, because they draw from the ḥelev. Likewise, they forbade threads (veins) and membranes that extend from the ḥalavim forbidden by Torah law, because they draw from them. As the Sages said (ibid.), there are five places that have threads and membranes that must be removed, three of them because of ḥelev – in the spleen, in the kesalim and in the kidneys. In various communities the custom was to be stringent regarding additional fats, because of their proximity to or resemblance to the forbidden ḥalavim.

In addition, in the wake of the destruction of communities and the exiles, doubts arose concerning additional fats in the animal's body, and in any doubt concerning a Torah prohibition one must be stringent. In doubts concerning prohibitions that are rabbinic or due to custom, it would have been possible by the letter of the law to permit; but in practice, because of the severity of the prohibition of ḥelev and the difficulty of distinguishing between ḥelev and shuman, the custom was generally to be stringent (below, halakhot 8-9).3

After separating the ḥelev from the other parts of the meat and the fat, one must put it in a place where there will be no concern that it will become mixed with the kosher meats and fats. Nowadays, when it is not customary to use ḥelev for candles and the like, the custom is to throw it into the place where the tereifot are put.

sections.title: The Prohibition of the Gid Ha-nasheh
sections.html:
It is a Torah mitzva not to eat the gid ha-nasheh (sciatic nerve) that is on the right kaf ha-yarekh (hollow of the thigh) and on the left kaf ha-yarekh of a domestic animal and a wild animal, as it is stated (Bereishit 32:33): "Therefore the children of Israel do not eat the gid ha-nasheh which is upon the hollow of the thigh." The gid ha-nasheh is the large sinew through which most of the nerves of the leg pass (the sciatic nerve). It begins at the spinal cord and ends at the end of the leg, and the Torah forbade eating the part that is on the kaf ha-yarekh, that is, on the rounded flesh that wraps the thigh bone, whose shape is like the ladle (kaf) of a pot, that is, a rounded shape that rises towards its middle. This kaf exists in all species of domestic and wild animal, whereas in fowl, even though there is flesh on the thigh, it is not round like a kaf but flat. Therefore, the gid ha-nasheh is forbidden in domestic and wild animals and permitted in fowl.

In a large ox, the length of the part forbidden by Torah law is at most eight cm, and in a large sheep – about four cm (Rema 100:1; Taz 3). This part of the sinew is easy to remove, because after the meat of the kaf ha-yarekh is taken apart, it protrudes from the meat.

The Sages added and forbade also the beginning of this sinew from the spinal column and also its continuation down to the end of the shank (shok). They also forbade the kenokanot (branches) of the gid ha-nasheh, that is, its branches that spread into the meat on the thigh. And holy Israel are accustomed to forbid also the fat around the sinew and the kenokanot. There is another sinew called the outer (ḥitzon) one, and the Sages forbade it as well. Its root is in the spinal cord, about two vertebrae before the beginning of the gid ha-nasheh, and from there it extends to the outer side of the meat of the thigh and penetrates into it (SA 65:8). This sinew is second in importance in conveying the nerves to the leg.

Removing all the parts forbidden by the words of the Sages and by the custom of Israel is a complex task that requires study – how to cut the meat in such a way that with relatively few cuts it will be possible to remove the sinew with its branches and its fat.

Even though the taste of the gid ha-nasheh is very faint, since the Torah forbade it, one who eats it with the thigh, even though he does not enjoy its taste, transgresses a Torah prohibition whose punishment is lashes. The kenokanot and the fat around the sinew, which are forbidden by the words of the Sages and by custom, do have taste; therefore, if they were cooked in a dish, as long as their taste is perceptible in the dish, the dish is forbidden to be eaten. The gid ha-nasheh is forbidden to be eaten and permitted for benefit (SA 65:9-10).4

sections.title: The Basis of the Prohibition in the Struggle of Yaakov Our Father
sections.html:
The basic reason for the prohibition of the gid ha-nasheh is explained in the Torah (Bereishit 32:23-33). After Yaakov our father was saved from his father-in-law, Lavan the Aramean, who sought to kill him, he began to prepare for the encounter with Esav his brother, who also sought to kill him. "And he rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two maidservants, and his eleven children, and passed over the ford of the Yabbok. And he took them, and sent them over the stream, and sent over that which he had." The Sages said (Ḥullin 91a) that he went back and crossed the river again in order to bring small jugs that had been forgotten there, because the righteous hold their money dearer than their bodies, since they do not stretch out their hands to robbery. "And Yaakov was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until the break of dawn. And when he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Yaakov's thigh was strained as he wrestled with him. And he said: Let me go, for the dawn has broken. And he said: I will not let you go unless you bless me. And he said to him: What is your name? And he said: Yaakov. And he said: Your name shall no longer be called Yaakov, but Yisrael; for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed. And Yaakov asked him and said: Tell me, I pray you, your name. And he said: Why is it that you ask after my name? And he blessed him there. And Yaakov called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved. And the sun rose upon him as he passed over Penuel, and he limped upon his thigh. Therefore the children of Israel do not eat the gid ha-nasheh which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day; because he touched the hollow of Yaakov's thigh, on the gid ha-nasheh." That is to say, by not eating the gid ha-nasheh, in which Yaakov our father was wounded, we remember his legacy – that with devotion and heroism he established the family of Israel and brought it back to the Land.

Even though the reason for the mitzva is connected to the event that happened with Yaakov our father, we were commanded not to eat the gid ha-nasheh when the Torah was given to Israel through Moshe our teacher at Sinai, and in the Torah the mitzva was attached to the narrative of the event in order to teach us its reason (Ḥullin 100b). However, it appears that even before the giving of the Torah, the members of Yaakov's family were accustomed not to eat the gid ha-nasheh, except that their custom was based on an inner feeling and not on a binding commandment (see Rambam, Commentary on the Mishna, Ḥullin 7:6; Hilkhot Melakhim 9:1, and Kesef Mishneh there).

sections.title: The Inner Meaning of the Prohibition of the Gid Ha-nasheh
sections.html:
The Sages said (Ḥullin 91a; Bereishit Rabba 77:3) that the angel who wrestled with Yaakov was the guardian angel (sar) of Esav, and their struggle reached up to the Throne of Glory, because it touches on the foundations of faith. The guardian angel of Esav wants this world to conduct itself according to its nature, whereas Yaakov our father wants to repair it through faith, values and Torah. And when the angel of Esav saw that he could not overcome Yaakov because of the strength of his faith, he struck him at his weak point, in the gid ha-nasheh; nevertheless, Yaakov stood firm against him and did not release him until he acknowledged him and blessed him.

The central nerves of the leg pass through the gid ha-nasheh, and spiritually, it is what connects the head and the heart, which express the thoughts and feelings, to the legs, which express the deeds. The blow to the gid ha-nasheh expressed Esav's claim: talk about faith and values is indeed lofty and beautiful, but in practice it is impossible to conduct the world according to the values of holiness, because in this world sins always overpower values and ideals. Not only that, but in the attempt to conduct the world according to the values of holiness there is an element of desecration of the holy, because the holy is meant for Heaven; therefore the righteous who try to walk in the ways of God in this world fall into sins. Nasheh denotes weakness, forgetting and change: in the transition to the legs and the world of action, good ideas weaken and are forgotten, and even change for the worse, since the gid ha-nasheh passes close to the place of desire.

The Sages said (Ḥullin 91a) that the reason Yaakov our father went back in the darkness of night across the river was to bring small jugs that had been forgotten, and then the angel attacked him. These small jugs allude to the weak and the sinners among Israel, whom Yaakov our father also did not want to give up on, because without them Knesset Yisrael is lacking and will not be able to repair the world. For their weakness is not due to wickedness of heart, but because their task is very difficult – to reveal holiness within practical and material reality – and sometimes, before they succeed in repairing all the material inclinations, the desires of the world overpower them and cause them to sin. The most precise place for striking at these souls in the body of Yaakov, the father of Israel, is the gid ha-nasheh, which is close to the place of desire, and striking it creates a disconnection between the lofty thoughts and feelings and the world of action with all its desires. This is what the Sages said: with the blow that the angel of Esav struck Yaakov our father, he struck the people of action who support the people of Torah, so that they would weaken and forget their partnership in upholding the Torah and would not support Torah scholars (Zohar part 1, 171a).

There is a further allusion in the gid ha-nasheh: despite its enormous importance, as the nerves to the legs pass through it, it has no taste. This is like the people engaged in the world of action, who many times, when they first wish to study Torah and fulfil the mitzvot, do not merit a good feeling, because this world with all its desires conceals the light of the Torah and interferes with the revelation of the delight and joy in the mitzvot. Like the arava (willow) among the Four Species, which has neither taste nor scent, yet it must be included in the Four Species, and the entire tikkun depends on it (Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 4:2-3). And since the people of action sometimes have no enjoyment while performing the mitzva, many of them tend to sin. However, in the end the sun shone for Yaakov our father and he overcame the angel; and so, in the end, the wicked of Israel will be repaired, the values of holiness will be revealed in the world of action, all the desires will be repaired and turned to good, and even the willow and all the barren trees in the Land of Israel will bear fruit (Ketubot 112b). But in order that we not be drawn after the weaknesses and sins, we were commanded not to eat the gid ha-nasheh, whose purpose is sacred – connecting the lofty values to the world of action – and eating it expresses the forgetting of the idea and its fall.

The Sages said (Bereishit Rabba 77:3) that the blow to the gid ha-nasheh struck "the righteous men and righteous women, the prophets and prophetesses, who were destined to arise from him (from Yaakov our father)". For without the people of action fully connected to them, the righteous cannot realise their ideas in reality, and the prophets cannot express the ideas of their prophecy in a stable and precise manner. As a result, sins prevailed and caused the killing of the righteous together with the rest of the people in the days of persecution and terror, when darkness covered the earth. Nevertheless, Yaakov our father stood heroically against the guardian angel of Esav until the break of dawn, and when the light began to shine, it became clear to the angel that Yaakov our father was right, and he was forced to acknowledge him and bless him. And the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children: that they will stand heroically against all who rise up to destroy them, until the light of their redemption shines forth, and all the accusers will seek to bless them, and the kingdom of wickedness will vanish like smoke. Then the sinew that was displaced (nashah) and moved from its place will return to its place, and the connection between the world of the spirit and the world of action will be made complete.5

sections.title: The Order of Nikur
sections.html:
'Nikur of the meat' (porging) is the task of cleaning the meat of the animal of ḥelev and of the gid ha-nasheh. In order to learn this important halakhic field, on which the kashrut of the meat depends, one must be thoroughly familiar with the internal organs of the animal, see in practice which are the forbidden ḥalavim and what are the gid ha-nasheh and its branches and its forbidden fat, and learn from an experienced menaker (porger) how the animal's organs and meat are cut in order to remove the forbidden parts. As the Rema wrote concerning the nikur of ḥalavim and of the gid ha-nasheh (64:7; 65:8): "And the order of nikur should be learned only by seeing it from an expert who is skilled in its nikur."

Since the laws of nikur are learned through tradition, the stability of their transmission from generation to generation was greatly harmed by the upheavals of the exiles. The longer the exile lasted, and the more cases there were of communities being destroyed and the transmission of their tradition being harmed, the more doubts arose in the laws of nikur, and in order to resolve the doubts, holy Israel needed to be more and more stringent. Thus we find that already at the beginning of the period of the Rishonim, because of the doubts, they tended to be stringent beyond what halakha requires. As Rabbi Yaakov son of the Rosh (who lived about 700 years ago) wrote: he copied into his book 'Arba'a Turim' (YD 65) the order of the laws of nikur that Rabbi Yitzḥak, author of the Ittur (about 850 years ago), had written, and at the end of his words he remarked: "This sage was stringent, and upon the one who is stringent may a blessing come." And Rabbi Yosef Karo explained in his commentary 'Beit Yosef': "Because of several places that he required to porge and remove, which have no foundation or root, as I explained each one in its place…"

Still, all of Israel used to slaughter and knew how to remove the ḥalavim, the gid ha-nasheh and the blood vessels, and many times women were responsible for the nikur of the meat and for kashering it of blood. As Rabbeinu Yeruḥam wrote (Toledot Adam Ve-ḥava 15:5, 14, about 700 years ago), all the poskim agree that women are trusted regarding the nikur of meat just as they are trusted regarding sheḥita. And there are Rishonim, among them Rabbi Avraham ben Natan (who lived about 800 years ago), who even criticised in their books the custom of women who tended to be overly stringent and removed permitted fats out of concern for ḥelev. On the other hand, in Sefer Ha-agur (composed about 600 years ago), he wrote about a certain fat in the area of the loins that must be removed, but many are not careful to remove it, "except for some worthy women who porge also the ḥelev under that membrane, and may their strength be firm (yishar koḥan)" (Beit Yosef 64:7; 64:12, 2).

The longer the exile lasted, more communities were destroyed, and by the time they recovered and established new communities, additional doubts arose in the tradition of nikur, and they needed to be more stringent, and the work of nikur already required great expertise. As Rabbi Shlomo Luria wrote (Yam Shel Shlomo, Ḥullin 1:2, about 450 years ago): although in the days of the early authorities they relied on any upright person for the work of nikur, now they do not rely on that, for "in the days of the early ones they were not so stringent in their nikur as now, for according to the law of the Talmud nikur is not so difficult; only they added to it afterwards, as the author of the Ittur was stringent in the order of nikur, and in the land of Ashkenaz they were more and more stringent in the matter of digging out the kenokanot, peeling the meat from the ḥelev, and several veins because of blood." And he went on to explain that most of the stringencies are indeed rabbinic, and for these one can rely even on one who is not learned; however, in these laws the rules are complex, and the public does not know what is forbidden rabbinically and what by Torah law, what is because of ḥelev and what because of the gid ha-nasheh or kenokanot and what because of blood; therefore one can rely only on a menaker who is known to be "a God-fearing man, and skilled in the work of nikur".6

sections.title: The Customs Regarding the Hindquarters
sections.html:
Because of the difficulty of the work of nikur, in many communities in recent generations they preferred to sell to a non-Jew the hindquarters of the animals, in which almost all of the forbidden ḥalavim and the gid ha-nasheh and its branches are found. The first to mention this custom (about 500 years ago) was the Radbaz (1:162), who wrote that this was the custom in Egypt, "and it is a fine custom, for not everyone is skilled in nikur". And the Shela also wrote that it is proper to follow this practice, and this was the custom in many communities in Europe. However, they did not establish it as a binding custom; therefore, when not enough non-Jews were found to buy the meat of the hindquarters, they went back to porging the hindquarters and eating their meat.

Forgoing the hindquarters is significant, since about half of the animal's meat is in it, and it also contains meat that is considered especially choice. However, the loss is not so great, because the more stringent one is in the nikur of the ḥalavim and the gid ha-nasheh, the more the quality of the meat around them is harmed, since it must be cut into more pieces, and larger areas of it are exposed to the air and must be soaked in water for the purpose of kashering and salting the meat. And the water greatly damages the quality and appearance of the meat. In addition, the effort involved in porging it is also very great. Porging one hind leg, mainly of the gid ha-nasheh and its branches, takes about an hour to two hours, and afterwards the meat remains so cut up that it is fit mainly for ground meat.

And some have the custom of selling most of the hindquarter meat to non-Jews and porging the choicer cuts of meat (fillet and sirloin), whose nikur is relatively easy and worthwhile.7

sections.title: The Jerusalem Order of Nikur
sections.html:
Following the encounter in Jerusalem of the Ashkenazi immigrants with the traditions of the Sephardim from the West and of the members of the Eastern communities, about one hundred and fifty years ago the Ashkenazi rabbis in Jerusalem established the 'Jerusalem order of nikur' according to all the stringencies of those of Sephardic origin, of the Eastern lands and of Ashkenaz alike, with most of the stringencies naturally coming from the communities of Ashkenazi origin, which had undergone more destructions and wanderings. And since the customs of all the communities were included in it, instruction went forth from Jerusalem, until over time the tradition of the 'Jerusalem nikur' became accepted throughout the Land and the Diaspora. In this nikur, about 13%-25% of the weight of the hindquarter meat is lost. Still, there are communities, such as immigrants from Yemen and Morocco, in which they continue to porge according to the tradition of their fathers without concern for the stringencies of the other communities. In these methods about 5%-10% of the weight of the hindquarter meat is lost, and one who wishes to rely on them may do so; however, in a hekhsher (kashrut certification) intended for the general public, the custom is to take into account all the traditions, as in the 'Jerusalem nikur'.8

However, when the Temple is built, speedily in our days, it will be necessary to decide all the doubts in order to define precisely which are the ḥalavim and the gid ha-nasheh, since in the shelamim, ḥatat, asham and Pesaḥ sacrifices it is a mitzva to offer only the ḥalavim on the altar, and it is a mitzva to eat the rest of the meat, and one may not be stringent with fats that are permitted by the letter of the law. And once again Torah will go forth from Jerusalem, when the Great Court decides all the doubts.
